title: Why Arjuna and Bhima fell
hookLine: Arjuna falls, then Bhima, who asks with his last breath why he is falling
carry: prasad: food offered first, then shared
tomorrow: will heaven let Yudhishthira bring the dog?

cards: Arjuna, who threw his bow into the sea, is still walking. He's the one who heard the Gita in the chariot, who won Draupadi at her bridegroom-choice, who fought through the war.
Then, on the high road, grief at his brothers' falling seems to catch up with him, and Arjuna falls too. Bhima, who has asked why each time, asks again.
A little later Bhima the strong feels his own legs go, and lying on the ground, he calls out one more question, this time about himself.

teach.b: About Arjuna, Yudhishthira's answer in Ganguli's telling has two parts. Arjuna once vowed to destroy all their enemies in a single day, and he didn't. And he looked down on every other bowman.
Yesterday's ranking, in an archer's shape. Then Bhima falls, and this time he asks about no one else: I'm falling too. Why?

teach.h: "YOU ATE WITHOUT A THOUGHT FOR OTHERS"
teach.b: You ate too much, you boasted of your strength, and when you ate, you never thought of what others needed. Then he walks on. Bhima's fault is the most ordinary of all: a plate.
And Hindu teaching has a great deal to say about a plate.

teach.h: GITA: EAT WHAT REMAINS AFTER THE OFFERING
teach.b: The Gita, the teaching Arjuna heard in the chariot, says the good eat what remains after an offering, and those who cook only for themselves eat sin.

teach.h: THE FIRST PORTION GOES TO GOD
teach.b: That's why, in so many Hindu homes, the first portion goes to God before anyone eats, often a small plate set before the shrine.

What comes back is prasad, food made holy by being offered, and prasad is always shared: with the family, the guest, the neighbor. Many families set aside a first roti for a cow or a hungry person too.
A meal eaten that way is the opposite of Bhima's. Bhima, who asked why every time, is the last brother to fall. Behind Yudhishthira now, only one follower is left: the dog.

how: The falls of Arjuna and Bhima are told in the Mahaprasthanika Parva. The Gita's teaching about food is lived in many Hindu homes: a portion is offered to God before the meal and received back as prasad, which is shared, and some families set aside the first roti for a cow or for someone in need.

o: the eldest Pandava, who leads the line and walks on
the strong second Pandava, who asks why each one falls
the archer who gives his bow back to the sea

games.q: the falls and the plate — tap the pairs.
p: ate with no thought for others
those who cook only for themselves eat sin
food offered to God, then shared

s: the brothers fall for terrible crimes
each reason is small: a boast, a scorn, an appetite.
Bhima asks about his own fall
lying on the ground, he asks why he is falling, and Yudhishthira tells him.
food offered to God is set aside and not eaten
it comes back as prasad, and it's eaten and shared; that's the point.

games.q: you're Bhima, falling on the mountain road. you've asked about every one who fell before you. what do you do now?
o: ask why you yourself are falling.
games.why: Bhima asks about himself, and Yudhishthira answers: too much eating, boasting of strength, and no thought for what others needed.

practice: Before your next meal or snack, pause before the first bite. Many Hindus offer the food first, with a quiet line or a small plate set before God, and then eat it as prasad. If you pray, try it that way today.
If you don't, name in your head three people whose work put this food in front of you, and share one bite of it with someone. Bhima's fall was eating as if no one else were at the table.

wordCard.voice: Bhima. The second Pandava, the strong one, who asks why each traveler falls, and falls last himself before Yudhishthira walks on with only the dog.

orig.note: Bhima: the second Pandava, the strong one, who asks why each traveler falls, and falls last.

carryVoice: Prasad: food offered first, then shared. Hold on to that one. Tomorrow, a king, a dog and a chariot from heaven. Day eight hundred seventy-six, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Mahaprasthanika Parva, the falls of Arjuna and Bhima and Yudhishthira's answers
